reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes an easy front-running bot that claims to automate profitable buying and selling, including potentially upwards of 1000 BNB per day. It directs viewers to deploy and fund a contract through a connected wallet and presents higher returns as dependent on supplying more funds, while the code, profitability, transaction outcome, and any viewer loss are not verified.

Today I'm gonna be going over deploying a front running bot on PancakeSwap with the Rapp B&B pair.
So the next step in this process is just funding your contract
The action button and then engages all the constructors that are built in as far as engaging a Pancake Router. It automatically buys and sells for you.
immediately buy and sell at profit

opening.argument: Judge, the description does not present this as effortless, universally compatible income. It warns that the contract will not work on Ethereum mainnet, explains that gas and burn fees can consume funds, and says that less than 0.3 BNB leaves little to work with. Those qualifications matter when assessing whether the speaker is concealing practical limitations. The profit claims deserve scrutiny, but the supplied material also gives viewers concrete reasons the proposed workflow might cost more or fail in the wrong environment.

citations.quote: NOTE: This contract have been designed for Binance Smart Chain and won't work with Ethereum mainnet (On UniSwap for example)
Gas fees average 0.06*2 (0.12 BNB as it needs speed to get in front of everyone).
If it targets token with 10% burn, that's another 0.03BNB taken off of 0.3BNB.
Less than 0.3BNB doesn't give you much to work with.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies funding instructions and a claim of automated profit. But its short profit quote leaves out the description's explicit fee deductions and chain limitation. Funding a contract is a risk-bearing step; by itself, it does not establish that the speaker concealed those risks or that the contract diverts funds. The supplied account does not verify profitability, but that evidentiary gap cuts against treating the claimed result as established, not automatically against the tutorial's stated purpose.

citations.quote: Gas fees average 0.06*2 (0.12 BNB as it needs speed to get in front of everyone).
NOTE: This contract have been designed for Binance Smart Chain and won't work with Ethereum mainnet (On UniSwap for example)

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The fee notes qualify the pitch; they do not neutralize it. The description tells viewers to supply at least 0.3 BNB and says the contract will buy and sell at a profit. The narration then claims a rapid return and suggests much larger daily gains with more capital. Nothing cited by the defense independently verifies the contract's trading behavior or the claimed proceeds.

opening.argument: Judge, much of the video is a first-person deployment walkthrough: the speaker creates a contract file, selects a Solidity compiler version, connects a wallet to Remix, checks the resulting address, and demonstrates the action control. That sequence supports reading the primary activity as an operational demonstration, even though the speaker also makes ambitious profit claims. The claim that transaction reports could corroborate past results is not itself corroboration; it is also a reason to distinguish what the speaker says from what this record proves.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening emphasizes the funding step and promised automation, but those occur within a narrated sequence of compiling, deploying, checking an address, and invoking a contract control. Calling that sequence instructional does not certify the code or the return claim. It means the presence of funding instructions alone does not settle whether the video's central purpose is a deceptive solicitation rather than a demonstration of the speaker's proposed workflow.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A walkthrough can still be a solicitation. Here the demonstrated steps lead directly to funding and activating the contract, while the speaker says it returns profit to the wallet and claims gains of several hundred BNB. The cited compilation and address check show parts of a deployment workflow, not that the contract performs the advertised trades or pays viewers.

opening.argument: Judge, the mechanism described is a user-operated contract funded from the user's wallet, not a stated payment to the speaker. The narration tells viewers to check the contract address and send funds to that contract, while the description says proceeds would return to the user's wallet. Those are claims, not proof the code behaves as advertised. Still, the supplied material does not identify a speaker-controlled recipient, a request for wallet credentials, or a recruitment requirement. On this record, the proposed transaction can be read as use of a trading tool without a demonstrated transfer to the creator.

citations.quote: we're going to deploy this to our wallet
So the next step in this process is just funding your contract, which is simple enough Let's go to your wallet
Make sure I got the right address in there.
automatically transacts back to your wallet 90% of the profit

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening's funding quote establishes a transfer into a contract, not who controls that contract's eventual outflows. The speaker describes deployment to a connected wallet and checking the address before funding it. The opening is right that the code and outcome are unverified; that same uncertainty means this record cannot establish that funds went to the speaker or that a credential-theft or recruitment mechanism was involved.

citations.quote: we're going to deploy this to our wallet
We can see that it's an address there now So the next step in this process is just funding your contract

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A speaker-controlled destination or credential request is not necessary to recognize the risk in this pitch. Viewers are directed to paste externally hosted contract code, fund the deployed contract, and activate it on the strength of claimed automatic profits. Deployment through a user's wallet does not establish what that unverified code does with the funds. The video's own claim of large returns with larger funding is central to the invitation.
